lessons.title: ভাবা (bhābā) — "to think," and the verb it was built out of
lessons.gloss: to think — and the machinery that made a "become" verb into a "think" verb

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You already have the verb "to be." Sanskrit built "to think" out of it, by a trick Bengali still uses every day.
ভাবা — bhābā — to think.
আমি ভাবি (āmi bhābi), "I think." আপনি ভাবেন (āpni bhāben), respectfully.
ভাবা (bhābā) is ভা (bhā) + বা (bā). ভ is bh, a b with breath behind it; ব is the plain b underneath. Two letters, one puff of air between them.

ভাবা (bhābā) is Sanskrit ভাবয়তি (bhāvayati), and bhāvayati is not its own verb: it is হওয়া's verb with a gear changed. Bhavati is "it becomes"; bhāvayati is "he makes it become" — and from making-something-be to imagining it is one short step. So Bengali bhābi and Bengali hôi are one root, √ভূ (√bhū), which is also English be and been, Latin futūrus (English future), and Greek phúsis (English physics). The noun bhāva, "a state of mind," sits between them: thinking is holding a state.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the gear that makes someone else do it

segments.text: Sanskrit changed that gear with a lengthened vowel. Bengali changes it with the ending -আনো (-āno), and it is completely alive:

utterances: plain verb: দেখা (dækhā), to see. the made-to-happen verb: দেখানো (dækhāno), to show — make see.
plain verb: খাওয়া (khāwā), to eat. the made-to-happen verb: খাওয়ানো (khāwāno), to feed — make eat.
plain verb: করা (kôrā), to do. the made-to-happen verb: করানো (kôrāno), to have it done.

segments.text: One suffix, and a verb you already own becomes a verb about making someone else do it. There is no separate word for "show" or "feed" to learn; there is a gear. That is the same machinery that built ভাবা (bhābā) itself, two thousand years earlier and one language back.

segments.instruction: the be-verb it was built from — "hôwā … āmi hôi"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the be-verb it was built from — "hôwā … āmi hôi"]

segments.instruction: see, then make-see — "dækhā … dækhāno" — and eat, then feed — "khāwā … khāwāno"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: see, then make-see — "dækhā … dækhāno" — and eat, then feed — "khāwā … khāwāno"]

segments.text: Which verb from last chapter shares ভাবা (bhābā)'s root? (হওয়া — both are √bhū; thinking is making something be.) What does -আনো do to a verb? (Hands the doing to someone else — দেখা "see" becomes দেখানো "show.") Give the Bengali for "show." (দেখানো, dækhāno.)

lessons.title: বোঝা (bojhā) — "to understand," the third knowing
lessons.gloss: to understand — the third knowing, and the harmony that this time moves the spelling

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Last chapter split "know" in two. This verb makes it three — and it plays the vowel game you already met, but this time the page tells you.
বোঝা — bojhā — to understand.
আমি বুঝি (āmi bujhi), "I understand." Look again at that vowel: not bojhi.
বোঝা (bojhā) is বো (bo) + ঝা (jhā). ঝ is jh, the breathy partner of জ — the j you met in জানা. And বো is the plain ব of ভাবা (bhābā) wearing the o-sign ো.

বোঝা (bojhā) is Sanskrit √বুধ্ (√budh), "to wake up, to notice" — the root that gave a prince his title: the Buddha is "the awakened one," and bodhi is the awakening. Understanding, in this family, is waking up to something.

Behind it is PIE bʰewdʰ-, and English holds two of its children: bid and forbid, from Old English bēodan, "to announce, to command" — a bidding is something made known to you. Greek took peúthomai, "I learn by asking."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the harmony again, and this time you can see it

segments.text: দেখা's rule was that the -i of "I" closes the stem vowel while the spelling stands still. Here is the same rule on a different vowel — and the spelling moves with it:

utterances: Bengali: আমি বুঝি. said: bujhi — the -i raises ো to ু.
Bengali: সে বোঝে. said: bojhe — stays o.
Bengali: তুমি বোঝো. said: bojho — stays o.

segments.text: Same law as dekhi against dækhe: the high -i pulls the stem vowel up after it. Bengali simply chose to write this one down.
And now three knowings where English has one: জানা for a fact, চেনা for a person, বোঝা (bojhā) for the thing that finally lands. ভাবা (bhābā) is the turning-over; বোঝা (bojhā) is when it arrives.

segments.instruction: the pair, then the older pair — "bujhi … bojhe" and "dekhi … dækhe"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pair, then the older pair — "bujhi … bojhe" and "dekhi … dækhe"]

segments.instruction: think, then understand — "āmi bhābi … āmi bujhi"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: think, then understand — "āmi bhābi … āmi bujhi"]
[YOU SAY: the three knowings — "jānā … chenā … bojhā"]

segments.text: Why is it bujhi and not bojhi? (The -i ending raises the stem vowel — the same harmony as dekhi against dækhe, only written down this time.) Which of the three knowings would you use of a person? (চেনা — জানা is for facts, বোঝা (bojhā) for grasping.) Which awakened prince is named from this root? (The Buddha — √budh, "to wake.")

lessons.title: পড়া (pôṛā) — "to read," and a letter Sanskrit never needed
lessons.gloss: to read — and the flapped letter Sanskrit never wrote

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: This word carries a consonant Sanskrit did not have. It is the sound of a whole family of words wearing down, and once you hear it you will meet it everywhere.
পড়া — pôṛā — to read, to study.
আমি পড়ি (āmi poṛi), "I read." সে পড়ে (se pôṛe), "he reads."

পড়া (pôṛā) is প (pô) + ড়া (ṛā). প is a plain p. ড় is ড (ḍ) with a dot underneath, and the dot changes everything: it is not a d at all but a flap — curl the tongue back and flick it forward once, as in the middle of an American ladder.

পড়া (pôṛā) is Sanskrit √পঠ্ (√paṭh), "to recite aloud" — reading was reading out, which is why পড়া (pôṛā) still covers studying as well as reading. And paṭhati became pôṛe by a rule that runs through the whole language: a single retroflex stop between two vowels softens into the flap ড়. That is why the letter exists; Sanskrit, which never softened them, had no use for it.

Watch it swallow a second verb whole. Sanskrit √পত্ (√pat), "to fall," went the same road — patati becomes pôṛe — so Bengali's "he reads" and "he falls" are now spelled and said alike, and only the sentence tells them apart. Past Sanskrit, paṭh goes cold: no secure Indo-European pedigree, and none will be invented for it. The falling twin is the rich one — PIE peth₂- gave Greek ptérón, "wing" (pterodactyl, helicopter), Latin petere, "to make for" (petition, appetite), and English feather.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the harmony, on a third vowel

utterances: Bengali: আমি পড়ি. said: poṛi — the -i lifts the vowel.
Bengali: সে পড়ে. said: pôṛe — the open inherent vowel stands.

segments.text: Third verb, third pair, one law: the high -i of "I" pulls the stem vowel up after it. দেখি against দেখে, বুঝি against বোঝে, পড়ি against পড়ে.

segments.instruction: "pôṛā" — read — then "āmi poṛi," flapping the ড়
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "pôṛā" — read — then "āmi poṛi," flapping the ড়]

segments.instruction: the three pairs — "dekhi … dækhe," "bujhi … bojhe," "poṛi … pôṛe"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three pairs — "dekhi … dækhe," "bujhi … bojhe," "poṛi … pôṛe"]

segments.instruction: read it, think about it, understand it — "poṛi … bhābi … bujhi"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: read it, think about it, understand it — "poṛi … bhābi … bujhi"]

segments.text: What is the dot under ড় telling you to do? (Flap it — curl the tongue back and flick, not a d.) Which two Sanskrit verbs both arrived at পড়া (pôṛā)? (√paṭh "recite" and √pat "fall" — the same softening ate both.) Does the reading twin have an English cousin? (No — the falling twin does: feather, petition, pterodactyl.)

lessons.title: লেখা (lekhā) — "to write," and the noun hiding in every verb
lessons.gloss: to write — and the dictionary form that is quietly a noun

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Four chapters ago you said dækhā hôbe and were told it meant "a seeing will happen." This word explains why that was not a flourish.
লেখা — lekhā — to write.
আমি লিখি (āmi likhi), "I write." সে লেখে (se lekhe), "he writes." The harmony, written down as in বুঝি: -i lifts ে to ি.
লেখা (lekhā) is লে (le) + খা (khā). ল is a clear l; খ the puffed kh you own from খাওয়া.
লেখা (lekhā) is Sanskrit √লিখ্ (√likh) — and likh does not mean "write." It means to scratch, to engrave. Which is what writing was.

Ask English the same. Latin scrībere, behind scribe, also began as "to scratch"; Germanic wrītan, behind write itself, meant "to score, to carve" — what you do to a rune-stick. Three unrelated roots, one picture. That is convergence, not kinship: লেখা (lekhā) and write are not cousins, and past Sanskrit likh has no secure pedigree. The finding here is a shared idea, not a family tree.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the dictionary form is also a noun

utterances: the same word: লেখা (lekhā). as a verb: to write. as a noun: a piece of writing.
the same word: পড়া (pôṛā). as a verb: to read. as a noun: study, homework.
the same word: দেখা. as a verb: to see. as a noun: a seeing, a meeting.

segments.text: Every -া form you have met does this. That is what Chapter 4's দেখা হবে was: not "we will see" but "a seeing will happen." It also builds nouns straight out of verbs — লেখাপড়া (lekhāpôṛā), "writing-reading," is the ordinary word for education. And the causative from three lessons back still runs on top: লেখানো (lekhāno), "to get something written."

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "lekhā" — write — then "āmi likhi … se lekhe"]

segments.instruction: the chapter's four — "bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the chapter's four — "bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā"]

segments.instruction: education, flapping the ড় — "lekhāpôṛā" — then "lekhāno," get it written
segments.source: [YOU SAY: education, flapping the ড় — "lekhāpôṛā" — then "lekhāno," get it written]

segments.instruction: the five you could already write — "ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch" — and which one wears the chandrabindu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the five you could already write — "ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch" — and which one wears the chandrabindu]

segments.text: What was দেখা হবে saying? ("A seeing will happen" — দেখা is a noun as much as a verb, and so is লেখা (lekhā).) Is write a cousin of লেখা (lekhā)? (No — both roots meant "scratch," which is coincidence.) What did দুই keep that Hindi's do flattened, who else in the east kept it, and did dv- survive in anyone's everyday numeral? (The -i after it; Assamese, Odia and Nepali; and no — only re-borrowings like দ্বার keep dv-.)
